sections.content: Wilmington, NC sits right where the Cape Fear River meets the Atlantic Ocean, and for real estate investors, it sits right at the intersection of affordability and opportunity. With a booming population, a major university, a thriving tourism economy, and a steady flow of military families from nearby Camp Lejeune, Wilmington offers something rare in today's market: genuine growth with room to profit. Whether you are just getting started or you already have a portfolio behind you, this guide breaks down how to find real estate deals in Wilmington NC and what you need to know before you invest. If you are brand new to the game, check out our full Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide before diving in.
Wilmington NC Market Overview: Why Investors Are Paying Attention

Wilmington is the largest city in southeastern North Carolina, with a metro population pushing past 300,000 and growing fast. The city has attracted major employers in film production, healthcare, tech, and logistics over the past decade. Companies like Novant Health and PPD (now Thermo Fisher Scientific) have created thousands of well-paying jobs, which drives consistent housing demand. The University of North Carolina Wilmington (UNCW) keeps a steady renter pool in place year-round. On top of that, Wilmington ranks as one of the top coastal retirement destinations in the country, pulling in buyers and renters from northern states every single year.

From a numbers standpoint, the Wilmington market has shown remarkable resilience. Home prices appreciated roughly 55% between 2019 and 2023, outpacing many larger metros. While the pace of appreciation has cooled with rising interest rates, prices have held firm. The median home price in Wilmington as of late 2023 sits around $350,000, though distressed and off-market properties regularly trade between $180,000 and $280,000, leaving real room for investors to find profitable spreads.

Best Neighborhoods for Real Estate Investors in Wilmington NC
Not all Wilmington zip codes are created equal for investors. Here are the neighborhoods generating the most investor interest right now:
Midtown Wilmington (28405)

Midtown is the sweet spot for flippers and buy-and-hold investors alike. You will find 1960s–1980s ranches and split-levels that need cosmetic work but have solid bones. ARVs in fully renovated condition regularly hit $350,000–$420,000, and rental rates for updated 3-bedroom homes run $1,800–$2,200 per month. Acquisition prices on distressed properties still sit below $250,000 in many cases, making the numbers work for both strategies.
Castle Hayne and Leland (28328 / 28451)

Just north and west of Wilmington proper, these suburbs are experiencing explosive growth. New construction is everywhere, but older homes on larger lots offer real value-add potential. Leland in particular has seen population growth of over 40% in the last decade. Rental demand is strong from families priced out of Wilmington's core neighborhoods. Investors can often buy here for 10–15% less than comparable properties inside city limits.
Ogden and Porters Neck (28411)

These northeast Wilmington communities attract higher-income buyers and renters. Properties here hold their value well and attract long-term tenants. Flips in this area can yield ARVs above $450,000 on the right home, though acquisition costs are higher. This is a better market for experienced investors with larger capital reserves.
Downtown Wilmington and Wrightsville Beach Adjacent

Short-term rental investors take note: properties within a 10-minute drive of Wrightsville Beach can generate significant Airbnb income, especially during peak summer months. A well-located 3-bedroom beach cottage can produce $40,000–$65,000 in gross annual rental income. Check local STR regulations carefully before pursuing this strategy, as Wilmington has been updating its short-term rental ordinances.
Types of Real Estate Deals Available in Wilmington NC
Wholesale Deals

Wholesaling is active in Wilmington, particularly in Midtown and the older suburban areas west of I-40. Motivated sellers include probate estates, absentee landlords with aging properties, and long-time homeowners sitting on deferred maintenance. Assignment fees in this market typically run $10,000–$25,000 per deal. If you are new to this strategy, our Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide is a great place to start. Before you put any deal under contract, run the numbers through our free Wholesale Deal Calculator to make sure the spread works for your buyer.
Fix and Flip

Wilmington's strong retail buyer demand makes it a solid flip market. Average renovation costs for a standard cosmetic flip run $35,000–$65,000, while full gut rehabs can approach $100,000 or more. The key is buying right. Flippers should target a minimum 20% gross profit margin after all acquisition, renovation, carrying, and selling costs. With ARVs pushing $350,000–$450,000 in many neighborhoods, hitting that target is absolutely achievable on the right buy.
Buy and Hold / Rental Properties

Long-term rental demand in Wilmington is powered by UNCW students, military families, healthcare workers, and young professionals. Average rents for a 3-bedroom single-family home run $1,700–$2,300 per month depending on location and condition. Investors should target a 1% rent-to-price ratio as a starting benchmark, though this is harder to achieve in today's market at retail prices. Off-market acquisitions are often the only way to hit that target in Wilmington right now.

Pro Tip: The UNCW student rental market peaks in January and August. If you are buying a rental property near campus, time your acquisition so you can have it rent-ready before the semester starts. A vacant unit in September can mean waiting nearly a full year to fill it at peak rates.
Key Market Trends Investors Should Know

items: Population growth continues: Wilmington added roughly 15,000 residents between 2020 and 2023, a trend driven by remote workers and retirees relocating from the Northeast and Midwest.
Inventory remains tight: Active listings in the Wilmington MLS have stayed well below pre-pandemic norms, keeping upward pressure on prices even as rates have risen.
New construction is not keeping up: Permitting activity has slowed, meaning existing housing stock faces less competition from new builds than in prior cycles.
Short-term rental demand is high but regulated: The city has moved to register and limit STRs in certain zones, so due diligence is critical before purchasing a vacation rental.
Flood zone awareness is essential: Parts of Wilmington sit in FEMA flood zones, and insurance costs in those areas can significantly impact your deal math.

sections.content: How to Find Off-Market Deals in Wilmington NC

The best real estate deals in Wilmington NC are rarely listed on Zillow or the MLS. To compete effectively, you need to go where other investors are not looking. Direct mail campaigns targeting absentee owners, probate leads, and tax-delinquent properties remain highly effective here. Driving for dollars in Midtown and the older suburban corridors can surface properties before they hit anyone's radar. Networking with local real estate attorneys, title companies, and property managers is also underrated — these professionals often know about motivated sellers before anyone else does. For a deep dive on finding these types of opportunities, read our guide on How to Find Off-Market Real Estate Deals.
Tips for Out-of-State Investors Targeting Wilmington

Wilmington attracts a meaningful number of out-of-state investors, particularly from the Mid-Atlantic and New England states. If you are investing remotely, here is what you need to know to protect your capital and move efficiently:

items: Build your local team first: Find a boots-on-the-ground real estate agent who works with investors, a reliable general contractor, and a property manager before you make your first offer.

Understand flood insurance costs: Get a flood zone determination and insurance quote on every property before finalizing your offer. In some flood zones, annual insurance premiums can run $3,000–$8,000, which dramatically changes your cash flow projections.

Use a local title company: North Carolina is an attorney-closing state, so you will need a real estate attorney to handle closing. Your agent or wholesaler should be able to refer you to a trusted one.
Visit before you close on your first deal: Even one trip to walk neighborhoods and properties will sharpen your judgment and help you build local relationships that pay off for years.
Analyze every deal rigorously: Emotions run high when investing from afar. Let the numbers lead the decision every time.

sections.content: The investors who consistently win in secondary coastal markets like Wilmington are the ones who build local relationships and buy off-market. By the time a deal hits the MLS, you are usually fighting 10 other buyers for a margin that barely makes sense.
